books.section: Topic 6.6 The Rise of Industrial Capitalism
America Transformed into the Industrial Giant of the World (1870–1910)
Industrialization, Corporate Consolidation, and the Gospel of Wealth

primary_sources: Andrew Carnegie, “Wealth” (The Gospel of Wealth), North American Review, June 1889

stimulus.text: The problem of our age is the proper administration of wealth, so that the ties of brotherhood may still bind together the rich and poor in harmonious relationship. The conditions of human life have not only been changed, but revolutionized, within the past few hundred years. In former days there was little difference between the dwelling, dress, food, and environment of the chief and those of his retainers. … The contrast between the palace of the millionaire and the cottage of the laborer with us to-day measures the change which has come with civilization. But whether the change be for good or ill, it is upon us, beyond our power to alter, and, therefore, to be accepted and made the best of.
stimulus.source_note: Andrew Carnegie, “Wealth,” North American Review 148 (June 1889). Public domain; wording and punctuation follow the original North American Review text. Ellipsis marks an omission between complete sentences.

stem: According to Carnegie, what is “the problem of our age”?

options.misconception: Carnegie wants wealth administered well, not ended.

options.text: The proper administration of great wealth

options.misconception: Carnegie says nothing about stopping cities in this passage.
Carnegie says nothing about the frontier in this passage.

rationales.A: Carnegie asks how wealth should be administered, not how to end it.
rationales.B: Carnegie opens by naming the proper administration of wealth as the problem.
rationales.C: Cities do not appear in Carnegie’s statement of the problem.
rationales.D: The frontier does not appear in Carnegie’s statement of the problem.
rationales.general:
Use Carnegie’s first sentence.
1. Carnegie opens with the problem of the age in his own words.
2. The problem is the proper administration of wealth.
3. His goal is that rich and poor stay bound together in harmony.
4. Background from the books: Carnegie gave away much of his fortune to libraries and schools.
Remember: the first sentence of a passage often holds the author’s question.
